Taylor Swift composed "Mean" entirely on her own, as part of her self-imposed challenge to write every song on her third studio album, Speak Now, without collaborators—a contrast to her earlier work that involved co-writers.

This solo endeavor began after she secured a publishing deal in Nashville at age 14 and evolved into a deliberate test of her abilities, spanning roughly two years amid her *Fearless* tour schedule, where she drafted lyrics in hotel rooms and other transient settings to capture unfiltered personal reflections.

From day one, Nicks was someone who could say what most struggle to put into words, operating somewhere between confessional and mythical. The place she operates in is entirely hers, making her music some of the most instantly recognisable and distinctive, with an added flavour of that quintessential Nicks allure that is hard to put your finger on.

Buckingham Nicks is the perfect place for any burgeoning Nicks fan to start, as it gives a glimpse into both her mindset as someone trying to make ends meet and her early abilities as one of the greatest storytellers in history.

Rumours is a must for any self-professed Nicks loyalist, as it's not only one of the best and most advanced rock efforts in music history but a major part of Nicks' personal journey with relationships, art, and, perhaps most importantly, herself.
Showing Nicks' ability to pour whimsical lyricism into heartache, heartbreak, longing, and desire.

Nicks' first solo album was a challenge for the singer, and while it's not perfect, the standout songs are. Others, like 'After the Glitter Fades', 'Leather and Lace', and, of course, 'Edge of Seventeen' became Nicks' staple solo songs, setting her on a successful solo journey that proved that, even if she still needed help and support from external figures, she always had what it took to make it on her own.
The Wild Heart saw Nicks pushing the boundaries of her own capabilities, weaving personal afflictions with creative storytelling to create her own carefully crafted worlds.

The standout, 'Beauty and the Beast', features an extensive orchestral section throughout, beneath Nicks' gorgeous vocals, which reached far further than the emotional appeal she'd used within the instrument of her own voice on previous records, Fleetwood Mac included.

Rock A Little proved the perils of pursuing a passion project while in the throes of something darker and more sinister. Listening now, you'd never know Nicks was struggling as much as she was, but that also enhances the mysticism of it – that Nicks was still at the top of her game, even then.
